title:
Comment of Chelsea McDonald in Docket(s)/Project(s) P-15423-000
Submission Date: 10/30/2026

documents.name: 151977.txt
documents.text:
Chelsea McDonald, NEW YORK, NY.
RE: Comments on Docket No. P-15423-000
Dear Secretary Reese,
Waterkeeper Alliance opposes the proposed DeepGreen Cook Inlet Subsea-Compute & Infrastructure Hub Project and urges the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC”) to deny DeepGreen Cook Inlet SPV, LLC’s preliminary permit application (Docket No. P-15423-000). The proposed marine hydrokinetic turbine array and subsea data centers raise serious concerns about potential harm to Cook Inlet’s water quality, marine ecosystems, and communities that depend on these waters. Although a preliminary permit would not authorize construction, we oppose granting the applicant priority to pursue a license for a project that could place these waters and the people and wildlife they sustain at risk.
Waterkeeper Alliance is a global movement uniting approximately 300 community-based Waterkeeper groups around the world, focusing action on issues that affect our waterways, from pollution to climate change. The Waterkeeper movement patrols and protects nearly six million square miles of rivers, lakes, and coastlines in the Americas, Europe, Australia, Asia, and Africa. In the U.S., Waterkeeper Alliance represents the interests of more than 160 U.S. Waterkeeper groups and their more than one million members and supporters that live, work, and recreate in or near waterways across the country, many severely impaired by pollution. Waterkeepers across the United States hold stake in keeping our marine ecosystems and our drinking water safe and clean. Our network includes Cook Inletkeeper, a community-based organization dedicated to fearlessly advocate for clean water, healthy ecosystems, and wildlife using science and outreach, protecting the Cook Inlet watershed and confronting toxic pollution and climate change.
In February, the company DeepGreen Cook Inlet SPV, LLC filed an application for a preliminary permit, pursuant to section 4(f) of the Federal Power Act (FPA), proposing to study the feasibility of a “Subsea-Compute & Infrastructure Hub Project” to be located in the Upper Cook Inlet, East Foreland Corridor, Kenai Peninsula Borough, Alaska. Although issuance of this preliminary permit would not authorize construction or land-disturbing activities, Waterkeeper Alliance opposes the proposed project and urges FERC to deny the preliminary permit application. Waterkeeper Alliance is particularly concerned about three potential environmental impacts: copper releases, underwater noise, and waste heat.
The placement of a hyperscale data center underwater is a relatively novel concept, and the full scope of its environmental impacts remain uncertain. This uncertainty is especially concerning given the proposed project’s scale, which includes approximately 330-350 marine hydrokinetic turbines and 66 subsea data center pods. Describing the facility’s cooling system as passive does not establish that it would be environmentally harmless, as transferring heat into surrounding waters and exposing cooling infrastructure to seawater may introduce risks that require careful, site-specific evaluation.
Cook Inlet’s waters support salmon, endangered beluga whales, and communities whose livelihoods and cultural practices depend on a healthy marine ecosystem. Potential copper contamination, acoustic disturbance, and localized warming must therefore be thoroughly considered, including their possible effects on habitat use, fish migration, and prey availability. As discussed below, existing research provides substantial reasons for concern about these pathways, even as the magnitude of this project’s impacts remains unresolved. Waterkeeper Alliance urges FERC to take a precautionary approach and deny the application rather than grant licensing priority to a project that could place these ecological and community resources at risk.
Underwater Noise Could Harm Endangered Cook Inlet Beluga Whales
The proposed project raises serious concerns about additional underwater noise in Cook Inlet, where endangered beluga whales depend on sound to communicate, navigate, and locate prey. The necessary surveys, installation activities, and supporting vessels to initiate this project and the operation of approximately 330-350 tidal turbines is likely to introduce acoustic disturbance into these waters. Although a preliminary permit would not authorize construction, the potential acoustic consequences of the project warrant consideration at this stage.
Research specific to Cook Inlet demonstrates the potential for human-generated noise to interfere with beluga communication. NOAA researchers found that commercial ship noise could partially or completely mask commonly used beluga calls at a study site in the Susitna delta, within the population’s core habitat. These findings demonstrate the importance of evaluating additional noise in an ecosystem where beluga communication is already subject to interference. FERC should consider whether project-related noise could mask beluga communication and echolocation, disrupt feeding, or discourage whales from using important habitat.
Research on tidal turbines also highlights the need to distinguish hearing injury from other acoustic effects. Researchers have raised concerns about behavioral effects from large turbine arrays. It has been examined how noise from tidal energy devices can reduce marine mammals’ “listening space,” with effects varying by device and species. Together, these studies show why findings from a single turbine cannot establish the acoustic compatibility of hundreds of turbines operating within Cook Inlet.
Any assessment should therefore address the proposed array as a whole, including the frequencies, duration, and spatial extent of its noise and its contribution to existing vessel and industrial noise. It should also account for seasonal beluga presence, feeding activity, and the acoustic characteristics of the project site. Waterkeeper Alliance opposes introducing an industrial facility of this scale into Cook Inlet due to its potential acoustic effects on endangered belugas. The possibility of adding persistent noise that interferes with communication, feeding, and habitat use reinforces our request that FERC deny the preliminary permit application.
Potential Copper Releases Threaten Water Quality and Salmon Populations

Deepgreen’s proposed project raises concerns about copper entering Cook Inlet from the facility’s cooling infrastructure. The proposed design would transfer waste heat through copper-nickel alloy cooling fins exposed directly to seawater. The combination of strong currents, suspended sediment, and thermal stress could cause potential copper releases. Before drawing conclusions about the environmental compatibility of this design, FERC should require information about the materials used, their performance under local conditions, and the amount and form of copper that could enter surrounding waters.
Copper exposure can harm salmon even at concentrations that do not cause immediate mortality. Research on juvenile coho salmon has demonstrated that dissolved copper can impair their sense of smell and disrupt predator-avoidance behavior. Studies have observed these effects at concentrations as low as two micrograms per liter under the freshwater conditions tested. Further research demonstrated that copper-exposed juvenile coho were less able to respond to predator cues and more vulnerable to capture by cutthroat trout. These findings illustrate why evaluating copper pollution requires consideration of behavioral and ecological effects. 
Waste Heat’s Effects on Salmon and Marine Habitat
The proposed facility’s passive cooling system would transfer waste heat from the data centers into surrounding seawater. Cook Inletkeeper has raised concerns about whether this could create a warm-water plume in the Forelands, an important passage for salmon migrating toward rivers in the northern watershed. The dispersion of waste heat into the cold sea is advertised by DeepGreen as an advantage, but the warming of the marine ecosystem of Cook Inlet very likely could have negative environmental impacts, affecting wildlife in the area. 
Research shows that Pacific salmon’s thermal sensitivity varies by species, population, and life stage, with temperature influencing physiological performance and behavior. It is vitally important given this research that whether a thermal plume could alter salmon migration or habitat use is carefully examined. Potential effects on salmon also warrant consideration because salmon are an important prey resource for Cook Inlet belugas. These unresolved thermal impacts reinforce Waterkeeper Alliance’s opposition to the project and our request that FERC deny the preliminary permit application.
Community Impacts
The proposed project’s benefits to Cook Inlet communities remain unclear. According to the notice, the electricity generated would primarily power the subsea data center, with only spare electricity potentially diverted to the local grid. The project therefore should not be presumed to provide a meaningful local energy benefit. Meanwhile, potential impacts on water quality, salmon, and marine mammals could place additional burdens on communities whose livelihoods, food resources, and cultural practices depend on healthy waters. FERC should carefully consider who would receive the benefits of this development and who would bear its environmental risks.
For these reasons, Waterkeeper Alliance urges FERC to deny DeepGreen Cook Inlet SPV, LLC’s preliminary permit application. Although this permit would not authorize construction, it would grant the applicant priority to pursue a license for a project that raises serious, unresolved concerns about copper contamination, underwater noise, and waste heat. Cook Inlet’s communities and ecosystems should not bear these risks for a development whose local benefits have not been clearly demonstrated. 
Respectfully submitted,
Waterkeeper Alliance
